words.definition: A situation in which people only hear opinions that agree with their own, so their existing beliefs are reinforced.
words.example: Social media algorithms can trap users in echo chambers, making them less tolerant of opposing views.

words.definition: False or inaccurate information, whether or not it is spread deliberately.
words.example: The rapid spread of misinformation during health crises can have life-threatening consequences.

words.definition: The presentation of news in a shocking or exciting way in order to attract attention, rather than to inform accurately.
words.example: Sensationalism in news coverage can distort public perceptions of how common violent crime really is.

words.definition: A popular newspaper with small pages, short articles and a focus on celebrities, scandal and dramatic stories.
words.example: Tabloids are frequently criticised for intruding into the private lives of public figures and their families.

words.definition: The right of journalists and newspapers to report news and express opinions without government control.
words.example: Press freedom is a cornerstone of democracy, allowing journalists to expose wrongdoing by those in power.

words.definition: Careful and detailed examination of something or someone.
words.example: Public figures must accept a certain level of media scrutiny as the price of their influence.

words.definition: An unfair preference for or against one side, which affects how information is reported or judged.
words.example: Readers should be aware of media bias and consult a range of sources before forming an opinion.

words.definition: Entering into someone's private life or affairs in an unwelcome way.
words.example: Intrusive advertising that tracks users across websites raises serious ethical concerns.

words.definition: Online content with an exaggerated or misleading headline designed to make people click on a link.
words.example: The pressure to generate advertising revenue has led some outlets to prioritise clickbait over serious journalism.

words.definition: An organisation, such as a newspaper, website or broadcaster, that publishes news.
words.example: Traditional news outlets are struggling to compete with the vast amount of free content available online.

words.definition: The collecting and reporting of news by ordinary members of the public, usually online, rather than by professional journalists.
words.example: Citizen journalism, made possible by smartphones, has allowed ordinary people to document events as they unfold.

words.definition: To have and use power or influence.
words.example: Social media influencers wield considerable power over young consumers' purchasing decisions.

words.definition: The control of what people are allowed to publish, broadcast or say, usually by removing anything considered unacceptable.
words.example: Online censorship is sometimes justified on the grounds of national security, but it can easily be abused to silence critics.

words.definition: Not supporting any particular side in an argument; fair and neutral.
words.example: Public service broadcasters are expected to provide impartial coverage of elections.

words.definition: To make something seem more attractive or exciting than it really is.
words.example: Critics argue that some films and music videos glamorise violence and drug use.

words.definition: To persuade someone to change their opinion or decision.
words.example: Targeted political advertising can sway undecided voters in closely fought elections.
